en: Tears will pour from his eyes.
Resting his chin upon your shoulder,
Buurul the horse will stand still.
Drawing in his belly and pawing the earth,
Buurul the horse will stand distraught.
Sniffing your right shoulder,
His eyes reddening like an argali's,
My dear one, when he sees you,
Making the cry of a foal,
Buurul the horse will stand sleeping.
Your bare red flesh,
Buurul the horse will sniff.
He has no tongue with which to speak,
That wise, distinguished creature among animals,
Whose aspect differs from all other beasts,
That distinguished courser among horses.
Say, 'He is my livestock inherited from my father,'
Catch Buurul and ride him home.
How your mother suffered torment,
Learn it from this.
Do not begin a war with the villains,
Only child of a khan's son.
I have chosen to entrust him to you;
Do not leave your Buurul behind.
Of Buurul, your courser,
Hear with sorrow the tale
Of this woman, your mother.
As Allah Most High ordained,
Let me tell how he was given.
Especially set apart for you,
Khan Saikal, daughter of Karacha,
Fought against your father.
When black night fell upon her head,
Left helpless, maiden Saikal
Offered Buurul as a gift;
Let me tell how she gave him.
Your father Manas was a hero,
An open-hearted lion;
His fortune lacked for nothing.
If you looked within him,
He was broader than the earth.
The horses grew fat and fit;
With your father among them, they numbered forty.
Hero Bakai, son of Oluyat,
Came and settled in Talas
And became Manas's companion.
Ajybai, son of Argyn Khan,
He too came to the Kyrgyz.
Chubak, son of Akbaltai,
He too came to Talas.
Almambet, son of Khan Azyz,
Warrior Shuutu, with a hat like a yurt's roof felt,
Yraman's Yrchyuul,
Baichoro of the powerful arms,
Tolok, son of Khan Tolgochu,
Adykhan's darling,
Akayar, who could lift a camel,
Tazbaimat, son of Khan Talaluu,
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty,
Akzholtoi, son of Adykhan:
All came to Talas
And became choros to your father, Sultan Manas.
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty:
The mad old man who grew puffed up at forty,
The old man whose every deed was strange,
The old man senior to the rest of the forty choros,
Who thought of being chief
And never gave up his mischief.
Until he died, that infidel
Never gave up his troublemaking.
Even if he let his gold flow away,
Noble Manas, that beloved lion,
Never said, 'He has ruined it.'
He first thought how to cause destruction;
Even if he burned his valuables,
Your father, like a swift steed,
Never said, 'He has ruined it.'
To your father lying in his great yurt,
He brought ruinous words.
At that very time, your mother
He utterly maligned.
'My Manas, have you learned what I know?
The prince's wife:
Can one who acts treacherously prosper?
One who calls a woman a human being—
Good heavens, can he be a Muslim in faith?
The crop that you sowed:
It turns out it is not your crop!
Chubak and Kanykei
Are not innocent, it turns out!
Of fierce Lord Manas,
Can one who enters his bed prosper?
Those who wish evil against his salt,
Choros, can they be Muslims in faith?
Can one who calls him a Muslim prosper?
And of Lord Manas,
Can one who enters his pillow prosper?
If you come near, does he rise?
Akbaltai's Chubak
Has acted like a beast;
Can he be a Muslim in faith?
Khan Baltai's son
Has robbed you of honor this year.
King Manas, consider it!'
When Kyrgylchal made mischief,
Your father blessed by Khizir, ah,
When he bitterly turned him against me,
Your heedless father, the lion,
Then me, your unfortunate mother,
It was there he tormented.
Believing Kyrgylchal,
He hung misfortune about my neck.
Your father the khan grew angry
And would no longer lie in my embrace.
I settled apart in the valley;
Neither dying nor vanishing, fierce woman that I was,
Because of Kyrgylchal,
I was a neglected wife for six months.
I did not sit looking on idly;
My soul was crushed with misery.
With your father the khan at their head,
I gathered forty dignitaries.
From the broad-jawed warriors,
And the unfailing champions,
From the skilled finders of sound reasons,
I gathered so many fine men.
Fat lambs and delicious heads:
I boiled them thoroughly.
'He will know my inward pain,' I thought;
Khan Bakai, born a leopard,
My uncle, I had brought.
Then Azhybai of the Argyn khan,
Shuutu the servant, with a hat like roof felt,
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty,
And Akbaltai's Chubak:
I had them brought expressly before the khan
And made my words plain to them:
'Sullen-browed Chubak in fine white trousers,
Now is the hour for your nobility, Chubak!
Secret talk about you has turned to slander, Chubak;
Perhaps our branch has broken this year, Chubak.
You became a son, Chubak;
I became a mother, Chubak!
You fled from Oigut and came, Chubak;
Like a doe I gave you my milk, Chubak.
A battle-axe is strong and cleaves heads, Chubak;
Running water is strong and breaks stones, Chubak!
A foolish man disrupts a people, Chubak;
Evil thoughts will never prosper, Chubak;
A troublemaker's fortunes will never double, Chubak!
They call what is made from white wheat flour dough, Chubak;
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty, Chubak,
Calls us two lovers, Chubak!
With your noble head and fine white trousers, Chubak,
You have become so grand and stately, Chubak!
While my sultan looks on, Chubak,
You have made a great mockery of me, Chubak!
A khan yourself, a sultan, what are you doing, Chubak?
While my blood-shedding hero looks on, Chubak,
Why make so many jokes at my expense, Chubak?
Seeing me here, you take liberties, Chubak;
Thus you bring me to ruin, Chubak!
If your generous hero rises in fury, Chubak,
You will go to your father, Khan Akbaltai, Chubak!
You will indulge your spoiled temper, Chubak!
You will indulge your spoiled temper, Chubak!
Your precious soul burning fiercely, Chubak,
You will turn back toward your people, Chubak!
A deep pit has been dug for you, Chubak;
Misery is boiling for you, Chubak!
Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty, Chubak,
Has spoken mischief about you, Chubak!
He has spoken words to ruin you, Chubak;
He has bent you to his purposes, Chubak!'
Lion-like Khan Chubak
Changed his aspect in anger
And spoke to Kyrgylchal.
His great teeth, broad as doors,
Shattered like millet grains;
Burning fire and flame from his eyes
Blazed beyond human sight:
'Hey, Kyrgylchal, leader of the forty,
Foolish old man who grew puffed up at forty!
Old man who acts the chief,
Old man rotten from the root!
The choros gathered together,
You meant to crush them;
Slandering them to my precious one,
The mighty warriors in forty directions,
You meant to scatter them!
Manas's heart, in this fashion,
You meant to cast down!
I have served the blood-shedding hero;
You meant to go away.
Setting him at odds with his wife,
You meant to go away.
Lying down or rising, always evil deeds:
You could scarcely restrain yourself.
Your mischief rose over your head;
You have been acting treacherously!
Ah, my friend, O Manas,
Knowing your nobility to be true,
I came to settle in Talas.
I too was a khan's son;
I too was one of the khans.
'Manas will know my worth,' I thought;
'He will take me out on patrol,' I thought,
And came to settle in Talas.
Suckling at Kanykei's breast,
I became a choro to Zhakyp's
Only son, Manas.
Could I prosper if I pissed upon my oath?
Could I be a Muslim in faith?
I have become utterly accursed; let me go.
What should I remain here for?
Ill-minded Kyrgylchal,
Let me bring you down as well.
I shall keep an eye on you, Kyrgyz;
I will not listen, Kyrgylchal,
To such crooked, confusing words of yours!'
Akbaltai's Chubak
Mounted and set out on his way.
Traveling without moving by daylight,
The renowned hero crossed the passes,
Crossed many lands upon his chosen course.
His wits fled, his eyes blazed;
Changing moods, his insides boiled.
Agitated, Chubak pondered much:
Upon Zhakyp's only son Manas,
'I shall bring some calamity,' he thought.
His thoughts were torn apart;
The tears poured from Chubak's eyes:
'O noble Prophet, my faith is pure;
I have seen little loyalty from people.
Perhaps our branch has broken.
We too were one of the khans;
Things went awry, we became dependent.
Alas, such is our fortune.
The son of a renowned khan,
He torments him,
Sparing none of his bitter slander.
This swine, leader of the forty:
What a dog's deed he has done!'
Akbaltai's lion,
Grimacing, terribly ashamed,
Not dying though disgraced,
Not simply dying of his distress,
At fierce Manas the lion,
Too ashamed to thrust his spear,
Wishing to die but unable to die,
Unable to take his own life,
His heart sorely shaken,
The tears pouring from Chubak's eyes,
He drew the line of his resolve:
Chubak, son of Khan Baltai,
To your fierce father, Khan Manas,
